# Self-Discipline and Goals

A consistent, intense streak of self-improvement runs through [[Traveler Stansberry]]'s private notes — recurring challenge regimens and rules he sets for himself.

## The regimens
- **75 Hard / 75 Medium** ([[75 hard 2025]], [[75 medium]]): self-imposed challenges — no nicotine/alcohol/weed/porn, work out 5 days/week, read every night, calorie/protein targets, strict phone-screen limits, and "lock in" on the IB diploma. The tone is unsparing: *"if I cannot do this, I am generationally cooked forever… consistency is key."*
- **[[lock in]]**: daily rules (homework before anything, no nicotine, pushups, sleep by 10:30, no weekday hangouts).
- **[[Opposite Action (DBT)|Opposite action]]** ([[opposite action (note)]]): a DBT-derived coping skill worked on in a session with **Dave** (inferred: therapist/counselor). The specific prescription: *"enthusiasm and participate 100% initially"* — i.e., when the urge is to disengage or withdraw, lead with full, genuine engagement instead. This is the one item on the list that comes from a *clinical* rather than purely willpower-based frame, and it suggests he sought (or was referred to) structured mental-health support alongside his solo discipline systems.

## What it reveals
A high-achieving, self-demanding temperament — and a habit of **externalizing willpower into systems**. This dovetails with his intellectual claim that *"strong is using willpower to overcome deterministic… tendencies"* (see [[Fate and Free Will]] and [[Intellectual Interests]]): the self-discipline isn't just habit, it's his lived answer to the free-will question he keeps asking in literature.

The presence of DBT work (opposite action, via Dave) adds nuance: he's not only imposing rules *on* himself from above, but also doing active therapeutic work *with* his emotional patterns from within. The two modes coexist.

# Homework Hatch (startup)

[[Traveler Stansberry]]'s real edtech/AI venture (2025–26), variously called **Homework Hatch**, **SPHW Buddy**, and **HW Buddy** — the concrete, real-world version of the AI ambition he keeps circling in his fiction.

## The product
An AI study platform that ingests a student's **LMS data** (Canvas, Schoology) and turns it into:
- AI study plans, summaries, practice quizzes (Kahoot/Gimkit-style), a class-focused chatbot
- A **college-acceptance-% calculator**, recommendations, test prep
- A gamified "**Buddy Coins**" arcade economy (coins earned by completing assignments)
- Class/grade/club chats

## Business thinking ([[prices]], [[idea]])
Three tiers — Normal $10 / Premium $20 / Pro $25 — with AI cost modeled at ~$2–3/user and hosting ~$2/user. The [[idea]] note includes a full ChatGPT-assisted pricing & break-even analysis (e.g. the "premium trap" problem). Tech stack surfaced in his notes: **AWS** (Elastic Beanstalk), **GitHub Actions**, **Playwright** (automated LMS login w/ 2FA handling), **Stripe**, iOS App Store release.

> [!warning] Security
> An associated note held **live AWS credentials in plaintext** and was deleted during ingest; those keys should be rotated. (Logged in [[log]].)

## Feature roadmap — sprint snapshot ([[sources/plan for next week (hwbuddy)]])
A near-term task list captured in an Apple Note gives the clearest point-in-time view of build status.

- New AI implementation (two passes — "implement new AI" + "improve AI" both checked)

## Building it for real — the ChatGPT build log (2025–26)
His ChatGPT export (51+ chats) turns Homework Hatch from a plan into a documented build. He shipped it largely by **"vibe coding" in [[Cursor (AI code editor)|Cursor]]**, then deliberately set out to *actually* learn to code so he could understand and edit his own app ([[Learning to Code for Homework Hatch - Beyond Vibe Coding (chat)]]).
- **Stack & deploy:** a **Flask** backend on **AWS**, evolving from **Elastic Beanstalk** → **App Runner + ECR** (he hit a 12 GB Docker-image wall), with **GitHub Actions** CI/CD, IAM keys, content filtering, and WebSocket config ([[Deploying a Flask App - AWS Elastic Beanstalk, GitHub Actions, and IAM Keys (chat)]], [[Fixing the Docker-to-ECR Push Failure for Homework Hatch - App Runner and the 12GB Image (chat)]], [[Launch to AWS Elastic Beanstalk - Flask Deploy and WebSocket Config (chat)]]). - **LMS ingestion — the pivot:** the plan relied on the **Canvas API**, but his school **revoked the API key**, forcing a pivot to a browser-extension scraper and cloud-storage OAuth (Google Drive / Microsoft OneDrive), where he ran into the OAuth consent-screen wall ([[Canvas API Key Revoked - Extension Scraper and LMS Access Strategy (chat)]], [[OneDrive Azure Integration and the OAuth Consent Wall for Homework Hatch (chat)]], [[Google Drive Folder Tree Mirroring for Homework Hatch (chat)]]). The sharpest psychological entry in the father notes is a short Apple Note ([[Dad on Change and Morality (Apple Note)]]) that makes two linked observations:

These two observations are related: if no one changes (and thus accountability is moot), objective moral standards become odd to maintain. Traveler is piecing together the logic of a worldview he can't inhabit.

# Emotional Life and Inner World

A synthesis of [[Traveler Stansberry]]'s most personal writing — the inner life beneath the high-achieving exterior. Drawn entirely from his own words and held without diagnosis; these are his self-descriptions, not labels placed on him.

## The recurring threads

### Emotional numbness / detachment
Across [[Halloween (personal essay)|Halloween]] and [[November 8th (journal)|Nov 8th]]: "I cannot force myself to cry… everything feels numb, like I am going through the motions." He notes alcohol is the one thing that "brings out the human in me" — both entries are written while mildly intoxicated, and he notes it each time.

> [!note] A partial contradiction on crying
> In [[Halloween (personal essay)|Halloween]] and the [[Emotional Detachment, Antihero TV, and His Father (chat)|Nov 1 chat]] he states he **cannot** cry even in "the most dire scenarios." But in [[November 8th (journal)|Nov 8th]] he writes: *"I start crying and wish I had worked harder"* — specifically in response to falling short of his own standards. These may not fully contradict: external emotional events leave him cold, but **self-directed shame at failure** may reach him where general stimuli cannot. The gap is real and worth holding.

### Three simultaneous failures — the Nov 8 triad
In one entry he names three parallel inadequacies: **squash** (athletic), **sociability** (interpersonal), and **feeling emotion** (internal). The fact that he treats the inability to feel emotion as the *same kind of failure* as getting cut from a team is itself revealing: emotional availability is something he expects of himself, and its absence reads to him as a deficit, not a given.

### Identity through intellect
"Then I found out I was smart. Really smart… I have made this almost my entire personality; for the sole reason that if I do not, I have no personality whatsoever." He processes **emotion through logic** — which, he admits, "makes utterly no sense." And in Nov 8th he makes the distinction explicit: his academic success came "because I was smart, and half the time I already knew what I was being taught" — not because of effort. Effort, in his model, is what he applies to *everything else*, and it sometimes isn't enough.

### Perfectionism & intolerance of failure
Getting cut from Varsity Squash senior year reads as a real wound: "Failure to me has always been unacceptable… makes me feel unworthy." He pushes back on his dad's *"there is no such thing as 'can't'"* — but also acknowledges that aphorism "guided my livelihood in my academics for the past 7 years," so the belief he intellectually repudiates is the one that formed him. See [[Fate and Free Will]] and [[Family and Personal Life]].

### The father, and the fear of inheritance
He calls his dad a **narcissist** ("hyper intelligent but… no empathy") — and the line that troubles him most: "I see some of him in myself." See [[Family and Personal Life]].

### Coping by hiding, then writing
The [[It's Not in My Control|avoidance]] he names elsewhere, plus [[When I Feel Like an Outsider|writing as his real voice]] — these essays *are* the coping.

### Drawn to morally-compromised characters
His love of *Breaking Bad* / *Dexter* / *Hannibal* ([[Film and TV]]) he reads as self-recognition — "bad people try to do good things" — and "trying to figure out which side I am on."

## The counter-evidence: [[Naomi]]
The numbness is not the whole story. With his girlfriend [[Naomi]], the guard drops entirely: after a moment of distress he writes that she "reach[es] inside of me and pull[s] out my fears, anxiety, and distress… you can get things out of me that most people can't." Both are self-described logical people who hide feelings; she's the one exception. If the numbness is real, so is the fact that **one person reaches through it** — which makes the looming [[Naomi|college long-distance]] all the heavier.

## How it connects to the rest of him
This is the emotional engine under the intellectual machine: the [[Self-Discipline and Goals|relentless discipline]] is partly a defense against the fear of inadequacy; the [[Fate and Free Will|free-will/willpower]] philosophy is partly a way to feel in control; the [[Faith vs. Knowledge|anger at God]] is grief about change he couldn't process. The mind and the feelings are the same story told two ways.

## The ChatGPT confessional (Nov 1, 2025) — the most direct primary source
The morning after Halloween of senior year, he used ChatGPT not for a task but as a **journaling/confessional mirror**, drafting and re-deepening an unflinching self-examination ([[Emotional Detachment, Antihero TV, and His Father (chat)]]). It corroborates and sharpens every thread above in his own real-time words:
- **The antihero pattern, decoded:** he wants *Breaking Bad*'s Walter White, *Dexter*, and *Hannibal*'s Will Graham to "win" because he wants proof that someone "most compromised in their own humanity" can still be redeemed — i.e. proof *he* can be. ## Context
Written "slightly intoxicated… in Cole's car." He notes he doesn't "really know how I feel" and keeps "trying to force myself to feel things." The past week's blow: **getting cut from the Varsity Squash team as a senior**, an event he explicitly frames as failure and inadequacy.

## Verbatim key passages

> "It feels weird to be constantly inadequate in the things I want to do. I want to play squash, I want to be sociable, I want to feel emotion; but I cannot seem to, no matter how hard I try."

> "My dad used to have a saying: 'there is no such thing as can't.' The older I get the more bullshit I think that is. Of course there are things you can't do."

> "I have always tried as hard as I could, and I've succeeded. But not because I tried hard; it was because I was smart, and half the time I already knew what I was being taught."

> "Failure to me has always been unacceptable. It makes me feel uncomfortable and unworthy, especially when I am a senior and can't get on the Varsity Squash team… I start crying and wish I had worked harder… I don't want to let anyone down, much less myself."

> "When I fall short of the expectations I hold for myself I feel inadequate."

## What it adds / corrects

### The three failures named together
For the first time in a single entry he lists three simultaneous perceived inadequacies: **squash** (athletic), **sociability** (interpersonal), and **feeling emotion** (internal). The parallelism is striking — he treats the inability to feel emotion as the same category of failure as getting cut from a team.

### Dad's aphorism — and the pushback
The verbatim saying: *"there is no such thing as 'can't.'"* He explicitly rejects it ("more bullshit"), but immediately acknowledges it "guided my livelihood in my academics for the past 7 years." So the very belief he intellectually repudiates is the one that drove him. See [[Family and Personal Life]] and [[Fate and Free Will]].

He credits his academic success to **native intelligence, not effort**: "I was smart, and half the time I already knew what I was being taught." This is notable for a student whose [[Self-Discipline and Goals|discipline regimens]] are intense — he distinguishes between effort-as-discipline (which he applies elsewhere) and effort-as-cause-of-academic-success (which he denies). The unspoken implication: squash, unlike academics, is a domain where smart alone doesn't win, and effort without natural ability fails.

### The crying — a small but real contradiction
He writes: *"I start crying and wish I had worked harder."* Elsewhere — [[Halloween (personal essay)]], [[Emotional Life and Inner World]] — he reports that he **cannot** cry "even in the most dire scenarios." Here he says he does, when he falls short of his own standards. This is not necessarily a contradiction (the Halloween essays may refer to *external* emotional triggers; this is *self-directed* shame), but it's worth holding: **failure at things he cares about may reach him where general emotional stimuli cannot.**

This entry confirms he was **cut from Varsity** as a senior — meaning either (a) the co-captaincy was of a JV/club team, (b) he later made varsity, or (c) the résumé overstates. The raw evidence here is unambiguous: "I am a senior and can't get on the Varsity Squash team."

# Halloween (personal essay)

One of [[Traveler Stansberry]]'s most vulnerable pieces. Ingested and quoted verbatim below; handled factually and with care.

---

## Full summary with key quotes

### The opening frame: antihero TV as self-recognition
He opens on his taste in TV — *Breaking Bad*, *Hannibal*, *Dexter* — and the realisation he arrives at:

> "I liked seeing bad people try to do good things. In Breaking Bad, we see a cancer victim become a drug dealer; in Dexter we see a serial killer act based on his 'code'; in Hannibal we see a mentally insane autistic man solve crimes with his incredible empathy. I always wanted the villains to turn good."

He then names what this was really about: "it's how I felt about my own life, and my fathers." The TV affinity is not casual — it is a **proxy for his own moral self-assessment**.

### Emotional numbness and social distance
A sustained self-portrait of feeling outside humanity:

> "I feel so distant from humanity sometimes that it makes me want to exit. Not the planet, or life necessarily, just social situations."

He catalogues what he thrives in alone — "learning, coding, gaming, watching movies and TV shows" — and what he can't access: "Girls, parties, spirit events; they always seem so distant from me, yet so close it's almost within my reach."

> "I can not force myself to cry, even in the most dire scenarios."

### The Halloween incident
The anchoring event: on Halloween, his father drove him and **8 friends** home **obscenely drunk**, doing ~80 mph on backroads at 12:30am. Traveler did not know his father was drunk when he called him for a ride:

> "My best friend's girlfriend left my house sobbing; we talked for hours about how my dad seemed to have no value in our lives as he drove 80 miles-per-hour on the backroads at 12:30 in the morning; I sat in my room trying to cry to resolve the emotion I felt. The tears form in my eyelids, yet nothing pours out. None of it affected me, not even enough to fake basic human reaction."

He ends this passage with a stark line: "I sit in my room writing this to display my intent to frame myself as a human, though I feel I have no reason to think of myself as one."

### Alcohol as emotional un-numbing
He is unusually direct about the role of substance use in his emotional life:

> "Alcohol does not numb me; it brings out the human in me. When I am mildly inebriated it is the one time I feel like I am being honest with myself, and when I have feelings. Otherwise everything feels numb, like I am going through the motions."

> [!note] This is a self-report about *mild* inebriation, not problem use. He frames it as diagnostically revealing — alcohol as the one pathway to feeling — not as a habit he endorses. Recorded as written.

### Identity-through-intellect, and the default
The clearest statement of how his academic identity formed by elimination:

> "I have never been athletic, so that defaulted me to academics, in my 7th grade mind at least. Then I found out I was smart. Really smart. Smart enough to piss off my teachers, and smart enough to get me in trouble for knowing the wrong things. I have made this almost my entire personality; for the sole reason that if I do not, I have no personality whatsoever."

He also notes the alienation of being high-achieving from the outside while empty inside:

> "I do well in school, I probably will get into a good college, I have good friends, I am the person everything thinks I am supposed to be. But I honestly have no idea who I feel like I am supposed to be."

### His father as narcissist — and the fear of inheritance
He diagnoses his father directly:

> "My dad is a narcissist. I am pretty sure, at least. He is hyper intelligent but seems to have no empathy whatsoever… He always thinks he is right, he feeds off of other people's acknowledgement of him, he constantly glorifies himself and his accomplishments; it's almost like there's no better word for him."

And names what frightens him most:

> "Wreckless, careless, idiotic, narcissistic: all of these things I see in my father. However, what is more troubling is that I see some of him in myself."

He also observes the contradiction of using logic to process emotion: "I have defaulted to using logic to process emotion. Which, in confession, makes utterly no sense considering logic and emotion are two completely different areas."

The closest thing to a confessional he wrote at the time — predating and shaping the Nov 2025 ChatGPT confessional chat (which re-tells the same Halloween night). The core architecture of [[Emotional Life and Inner World]] is traceable here: numbness, intellect-as-personality-substitute, alcohol as emotional un-locker, and the father-inheritance fear. # Memory and Trauma

How the past refuses to stay past — a theme Traveler reads as both psychological wound and narrative structure.

## Key readings
- **[[Beloved]]**: memory as trauma; Beloved as the embodiment of slavery, history, and "trauma" that re-dehumanizes Paul D. Morrison's "rememory."
- **[[Home (novel)|Home]]**: Frank Money's PTSD, hallucinations, and alcoholism; "going home" as a "physical rebirth of his soul," the Lotus as a symbol of rebirth and cleansing. Trauma healed through return and care.
- **[[Maus]]**: the Holocaust transmitted across generations (Vladek → Artie); the ethics of representing atrocity ([[Art as Survival]]).
- **[[The Narrow Road to the Deep North]]**: the POW camp and "the line" as trauma that fixes or frees identity.

## Structural insight
He notices trauma **deforms narrative form**, not just characters — e.g. Flanagan's non-linear "circle" chronology mirrors how the traumatized mind moves through time (see [[Fate and Free Will]]).

## The personal dimension — Scout
The theme isn't only literary for him. A 2025 Apple Note ([[Writing Idea — Scout (apple note)]]) identifies **Scout** — a pet from before his parents' divorce — as *"the one remainder from my past life with mom and dad."* Scout is exactly the kind of object his literary analysis keeps finding: an ordinary, living thing that carries a whole lost world. He flags it as a writing idea but (in the available sources) never writes the essay. The gap between *noticing* the image and being able to *execute* it is itself a data point. See [[Family and Personal Life]].
